#7693. Maryland Man Convicted of $18.7 Million Medicare Fraud for Respiratory Testing Scheme Targeting Nursing Homes

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

A federal jury in the District of Maryland convicted a laboratory owner yesterday for taking advantage of nursing homes that needed COVID-19 tests during the pandemic and fraudulently billing Medicare more than $18 million for other expensive respiratory tests that nursing home residents did not need, physicians did not order, and, in many cases, were never performed.

“Mr. Britton-Harr’s decision to exploit elderly nursing‑home residents and inexperienced interns for personal gain during a global pandemic is unconscionable. This verdict reinforces our message: there is nowhere to hide for those who commit fraud. We will find you and prosecute you to the fullest extent of the law,” said U.S. Attorney Kelly O. Hayes for the District of Maryland. “The U.S. Attorney’s Office, along with our law-enforcement partners, remains committed to rooting out fraud and holding accountable those who exploit our vulnerable victims and who steal our taxpayer money.”

“This verdict sends a clear message: the FBI will aggressively pursue anyone who steals from American taxpayers,” said FBI Baltimore Special Agent in Charge Jimmy Paul. “Patrick Britton-Harr will now face the consequences of his greed and brazen crimes. In addition to this healthcare fraud scheme, Britton-Harr was previously convicted for investment fraud in which the FBI uncovered a separate scheme where he defrauded private citizens. The FBI and our law enforcement partners will not rest until fraudsters like Mr. Britton Harr are brought to justice.”

According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Patrick Britton-Harr, 42, of Annapolis, offered COVID-19 tests to nursing homes across the country in 2020 when these facilities were desperate for COVID-19 testing services. After specimens were collected from nursing home residents and other laboratories performed COVID-19 testing, Britton-Harr billed Medicare for separate, high-priced respiratory pathogen panel (RPP) tests purportedly conducted in a laboratory he owned in Arizona. Britton-Harr falsely claimed to Medicare that treating physicians ordered these extensive RPP tests, which screened for more than 30 respiratory pathogens. In reality, physicians never ordered the tests for their nursing home patients, and several physicians testified at trial they had never ordered an RPP test for any patient during the entirety of their medical careers.

Through his company, Provista Health, Britton-Harr fraudulently billed Medicare $18.7 million for RPP testing purportedly performed in just six months, of which Medicare paid more than $7.2 million. Evidence at trial demonstrated how Britton-Harr exploited inexperienced employees, including a family member and high school and college aged interns, by directing them to bill Medicare for an RPP test every time a COVID-19 test was performed. Britton-Harr further directed the billing of RPP tests supposedly performed at his Arizona laboratory after he had already closed the laboratory, barred staff from working in the laboratory, and no longer had the equipment necessary to run RPP tests. Additional evidence at trial proved that Britton-Harr billed Medicare for RPP tests that were never performed, including billing for tests for nursing home residents who were already deceased.

Britton-Harr used the proceeds of his fraud scheme to fund a lavish lifestyle, purchasing, among other things, a $112,500 Porsche 911, and making $25,000 monthly mortgage payments on his Annapolis waterfront mansion.

The jury convicted Britton-Harr of five counts of health care fraud and one count of transactional money laundering. Britton-Harr faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison for each count. A sentencing hearing will be scheduled at a later date. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

Trial Attorney Chris Wenger of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Ari Evans for the District of Maryland are prosecuting the case.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

The Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit.

#7692. Crime Is Down: Why Leadership Matters

For years, Americans were told by the left that rising crime was either exaggerated, the result of poverty, caused by COVID, or simply the unavoidable cost of modern life. None of those assertions is true.

Victims, police officers, prosecutors, and families living in high-crime neighborhoods knew better. They understood that crime is not an abstraction. It is a stolen vehicle, a broken window, a family traumatized by violence, or a neighborhood slowly surrendered to fear.

That is why the preliminary results of the just-released 2025 National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) deserve serious attention. The numbers point in one direction: crime fell substantially across nearly every major category measured by the survey.

The results are preliminary, and responsible observers will await final estimates and additional analysis. But the trend is unmistakable—and it coincides with a national agenda that has placed public safety, border security, law enforcement, and support for victims at the center of federal policy.

According to the preliminary estimates from the Bureau of Justice Statistics, the rate of serious violent victimization—violent crime excluding simple assault—fell 25%, from 9.9 victimizations per 1,000 people age 12 or older in 2024 to 7.4 per 1,000 in 2025. Aggravated assault declined even more sharply, dropping 31% from 4.5 to 3.1 per 1,000.

>>> Americans Lost Over $20 Billion to One Type of Crime. Here’s How We Can Fight It

The property-crime figures are equally striking. Property victimization declined 19%, from 138.0 per 1,000 households to 111.2 per 1,000. Burglary or trespassing fell 25%. Motor vehicle theft declined 30%, representing approximately 349,000 fewer stolen vehicles. Other household theft declined 19%, while burglary and trespassing represented roughly 460,000 fewer victimizations.

These are not minor statistical adjustments. They represent fewer people harmed, fewer families disrupted, and fewer communities forced to absorb the economic and emotional costs of crime.

The NCVS is particularly important because it captures criminal victimization whether or not the victim reported the offense to police. Each year, the Bureau of Justice Statistics gathers information from a nationally representative sample of approximately 240,000 people age 12 or older in about 150,000 households.

It therefore complements the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting data, which are based primarily on information supplied by law enforcement agencies.

The two measures tell a consistent story. The FBI’s 2025 data showed the largest year-to-year decline in violent crime since the agency began tracking national crime trends in 1936. Murder and non-negligent manslaughter declined by an estimated 18.1%.

The NCVS now provides an important second measure, reflecting the experiences of victims themselves.

What explains the decline? No serious analyst should pretend that a single policy produces every change in national crime. Crime rates are influenced by many factors, including local policing strategies, prosecution decisions, economic conditions, demographics, and community involvement. Preliminary survey results also cannot establish a definitive cause-and-effect relationship.

But policy choices matter. A president who makes securing the border a priority, removes violent illegal aliens who are subject to deportation, directs the Justice Department to cooperate with the nation’s approximately 18,000 police departments, 3,400 sheriffs’ offices, and 2,300 elected district attorneys, funds law enforcement, and supports victims is sending a clear message: the government’s first responsibility is to protect the innocent.

>>> Another Win for the Task Force To Eliminate Fraud

That message matters. Criminals should expect enforcement, not indulgence. Police officers should know that federal officials recognize the risks they face. Prosecutors should have the resources and cooperation necessary to hold dangerous offenders accountable. Victims should not be treated as an afterthought in a system more concerned with the comfort of defendants than the security of communities.

“This report is proof that President Trump’s ’Make America Safe Again’ agenda is working,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said, the No. 3 official in the Justice Department.

The statement captures the broader significance of the data, even if conclusions should await final estimates: public safety improves when government treats it as a core mission rather than a campaign slogan.

The lesson is straightforward. Effective enforcement, cooperation among federal, state, and local authorities, secure borders, adequately funded police departments, and meaningful support for victims are not outdated ideas. They are practical necessities.

Americans should celebrate these preliminary gains while remaining vigilant. The goal is not merely to report that crime has fallen. The goal is to ensure that it stays down—and that every community, regardless of size or location, receives the protection its residents deserve.

#7689. Disability Discrimination and Allegations of AI Use in Student's University of Michigan Course Papers

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

"[A]t this stage of the case, ... [plaintiff] plausibly pleads that [the university] discriminated against her by disregarding [her medial records] to find that she used AI when the writing style of the course papers could have resulted from her disabilities."

From Doe v. Regents of Univ. of Mich., decided yesterday by Judge Laurie J. Michelson (E.D. Mich.):

Plaintiff Jane Doe filed this lawsuit against the University of Michigan and several individual defendants after she was disciplined for her alleged use of AI to write course papers. Plaintiff, who has generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), maintains that the "tone, meticulous structure, [and] stylistic consistency" of her writing can be misinterpreted as AI. Unconvinced, Defendants sanctioned Plaintiff with disciplinary probation and required her to rewrite those course papers and write a reflective essay. After challenging that discipline without success, Plaintiff filed suit, asserting claims under the due process clause, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), and the Rehabilitation Act (RA). …

This dispute unfolded last fall when Plaintiff was an undergraduate student in Great Books 191, a classical studies course at the University of Michigan. The class was taught by Theo Nash, the course's graduate student instructor, and Basil Duffalo, the lead instructor. According to Plaintiff, Nash made public "statements reflecting a predisposition to assume AI misuse by students and to treat AI-related concerns as a core academic 'values' issue."

The issues at the heart of this case started when Nash filed an academic misconduct accusation with the Office of Student Academic Affairs (OSAA), indicating he was "immediately suspicious" Plaintiff had used AI to write a course paper. Plaintiff denied that accusation, "explaining that [her] disability-related writing traits could be misinterpreted as AI and should not be treated as proof of misconduct."

Plaintiff participated in a conference with OSAA and submitted materials supporting that position. Not long after, Nash filed a second misconduct accusation based on another paper written by Plaintiff. He attached "AI-generated comparison outputs created by prompting AI with [Plaintiff's] own outline and with instructor feedback." Before OSAA's involvement on this second accusation, Nash asked Plaintiff to meet. Plaintiff declined. In Plaintiff's telling, Nash "interpreted her declination as 'self-destructive' and a refusal of help." Plaintiff then went through the same OSAA proceeding for the second accusation. OSAA found Plaintiff responsible for both accusations and sanctioned her with disciplinary probation (notated on her unofficial transcript) and also required her to write a reflective essay.

Five days later, Nash filed a third misconduct accusation with OSAA for another paper written by Plaintiff. Plaintiff again submitted materials to OSAA including "written notices" "explaining that an NR grade was blocking degree requirements and graduation and that her transcript and future educational opportunities were being harmed immediately."

Before OSAA adjudicated the third accusation, Plaintiff filed a complaint with the Dean of the College of Literature, Science, and the Arts, and the University President's Office, "about disability discrimination, retaliation, harassment, and lack of procedural neutrality in the OSAA process." The University responded that Plaintiff could appeal OSAA's findings, which Plaintiff soon did. That same day, Plaintiff filed a complaint with the U.S. Department of Education and the University's Equity, Civil Rights, and Title IX Office (ECRT). OSAA, in turn, paused Plaintiff's appeal pending ECRT's review.

ECRT dismissed Plaintiff's complaint given her approved accommodations. With that decision complete, OSAA then issued the same misconduct finding for the third accusation. Plaintiff was also required to rewrite course papers for Great Books 191.

In Plaintiff's view, Defendants "treated disability-related traits and limitations as evidence of guilt and failed to apply disability-informed modifications in the academic integrity process." That led Plaintiff to file this lawsuit. Plaintiff brings her claims against the Regents of the University of Michigan ("the University") and several individual defendants in their official and individual capacities, including Nash and Duffalo, and Sean Edgerton and Christine O'Neil from OSAA. …

The court held the individual defendants were entitled to qualified immunity as to the due process claim, since any alleged constitutional violation wouldn't be "clear to a reasonable" government official; an excerpt:

Based on the allegations in the complaint, Nash (and Duffalo) were faced with course papers that resembled the use of AI. Plaintiff has provided no case suggesting it would be "clear to a reasonable" university instructor that using AI-detection software to analyze that writing and bring an academic misconduct allegation as a result of that analysis would violate a student's procedural due process rights….

And the court rejected the due process claim against the institution:

[Plaintiff] was advised of the accusations that she used AI to write course papers. Her sanctions included disciplinary probation notated on her unofficial transcript, a requirement to write a reflective essay, and rewriting course papers. But before they were imposed, Plaintiff was given opportunities to provide her side of the story, including that her GAD and OCD caused writing traits that could be mistaken for AI. She provided medical documentation to OSAA, and OSAA expressly considered that information in its decision. In effect, Plaintiff "admits that [s]he received exactly the due process [s]he requested."

Pivoting from the process provided, Plaintiff maintains that OSAA's sanctions "rested on Nash's self-confirming AI comparison outputs." That argument is unsupported by Plaintiff's allegations and exhibits. Again, they show that OSAA considered Nash's conclusions against Plaintiff's explanations. And when forming its decision, OSAA even credited information Plaintiff provided that sufficiently disputed one of Nash's conclusions … ("In your evidence you indicated that the idea of the 'rat king' was something talked about in your discussion section which we were able to confirm.")….

All told, "[w]hen assessing whether an academic dismissal constituted a due process violation, '[a] court must 'show great respect for the faculty's professional judgment' and may not 'override' that judgment 'unless it is such a substantial departure from accepted academic norms as to demonstrate that the … committee responsible did not actually exercise professional judgment.'" The parties rely on this academic-dismissal standard even though this case involves assessing whether a disciplinary probation notation on an unofficial transcript and a requirement to write a reflective essay and rewrite course papers constitute a due process violation. But based on the allegations in the complaint and attached exhibits, the Court cannot find that Defendants departed from accepted academic norms or failed to exercise professional judgment.

The court also rejected plaintiff's claims that the university failed to accommodate her disability, and that the university retaliated against her for asserting rights related to her disability. But it allowed plaintiff's intentional disability discrimination claim to go forward:

[Plaintiff] describes the discrimination theory in her response brief as follows:

Nash's public statements reflecting a 'paranoid' predisposition to find AI everywhere, combined with his decision to file three successive accusations grounded in the very writing traits Plaintiff's clinicians had warned would be misinterpreted, and OSAA's decision to sustain those findings while disregarding the clinical record, collectively support an inference of intentional discrimination.

For their part, Defendants do not advance significant argument on this claim[, arguing instead that] … "With respect to the denominated claims of 'discrimination,' the Complaint does not actually contain any allegations of direct (i.e., intentional) discrimination. For that reason and to that extent, Claims I and II should be dismissed." … Yet Plaintiff maintains that her discrimination claims "are supported by allegations of intentional … discrimination." …

There can be no dispute that Plaintiff pleads Nash's "paranoid' predisposition" to find AI, and her submission of clinical evidence explaining why, given her disabilities, her writing style might be misinterpreted as coming from the use of AI. It is also true that the exhibits Plaintiff attached to her response brief that the parties are treating as integral to the allegations in the complaint, show that OSAA reviewed her clinical record.

But at this stage of the case, the Court must accept as true Plaintiff's allegation that OSAA disregarded the medical evidence. In other words, although Defendants considered and/or reviewed Plaintiff's medical records, she plausibly pleads that they discriminated against her by disregarding them to find that she used AI when the writing style of the course papers could have resulted from her disabilities.

Plaintiff further alleges that she provided Nash and Duffalo with information about her disability accommodations such that they were on notice of her disabilities. She pleads that she rejected Nash's request to meet with him outside of OSAA. Taking these allegations as true and drawing reasonable inferences in Plaintiff's favor, that rejection likely resulted from the effects of her disabilities, including difficulty with "live verbal defense, rapid processing, and adversarial questioning."

Indeed, that is seemingly why "Plaintiff requested that OSAA permit her to present her defenses in writing rather than through additional live Zoom proceedings, consistent with her disability-related limitations." But Nash, according to the allegations, interpreted Plaintiff's rejection of his request to meet as "self-destructive" and then followed up with another misconduct accusation to OSAA. Accepting these allegations as true, combined with Plaintiff's allegations about Nash's "'paranoid' predisposition" to find AI, Plaintiff plausibly pleads a claim for disability discrimination under the ADA/RA.

#7688. The Surprising New Guardians Of Liberty And What It Means For The Left

For years, the Left assumed Gen Z would be its most loyal supporters. Young Americans were expected to embrace socialism, distrust our institutions, and see government as the answer to the challenges facing our generation. But that assumption is increasingly being challenged by young people questioning the Left’s worldview and rediscovering the principles that made America exceptional.

The Left’s response has been revealing. Rather than defend its ideas, some of its most prominent voices are threatening the young Americans who dare to oppose them.

Recent remarks by Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) offer a particularly alarming example.

Speaking about holding Trump administration officials accountable, Slotkin described using corruption cases to deter young Americans from joining the administration. She said she wanted prospective employees to worry that serving the Trump administration could mean buying themselves “a ton of problems.” Her stated goal was to discourage young people from getting involved.

Consider what that means for young Americans who want to serve their country by working for an administration, organization, or cause they believe in. The message is that choosing to build a career in the conservative movement could put a target on your back when the opposing side regains power.

>>> Dear Gen Z: Reagan Is Not a Relic

What an abhorrent message. Young Americans should be free to stand up for their convictions and pursue public service without fearing that their political affiliations could make them targets of the Left’s lawfare.

There is a world of difference between prosecuting actual criminal conduct and using the threat of prosecution to discourage participation in the political process. The justice system exists to enforce the law, not to intimidate political opponents or make an example of people whose political affiliations dissent from those in power.

Slotkin may frame her proposal as accountability. But when the stated objective is to deter young Americans from serving their nation, the question is whether the pursuit of justice is being conflated with the pursuit of political power.

Young Americans should find that deeply troubling, regardless of their political affiliation. And for a generation already questioning the Left’s vision for America, these remarks should prompt an even more fundamental question: Why should young people trust a political movement that seems willing to threaten their futures when they reject its ideas?

For years, the Left has presented socialism as a compassionate alternative to America’s founding principles. It promises equality through government control, security through dependence on the state, and progress through the expansion of political power. But beneath those promises lies a fundamental disagreement about human nature, individual liberty, and the proper role of government.

The American experiment rests on a different premise: that our rights come from our Creator, not the government, and that individuals—not political elites—should have the freedom to direct their own lives. Free enterprise, limited government, individual responsibility, and strong families are not outdated obstacles to progress. They are essential to preserving a free and prosperous society.

Socialism asks Americans to place greater trust in government. The American tradition asks government to respect the freedom and dignity of its citizens. One concentrates power in political institutions; the other recognizes that power must be limited to protect individual liberty.

For Gen Z, this is more than an abstract ideological debate. It is a question of what kind of country we want them to inherit—and whether they will be free to shape its future. Will they embrace a system that increasingly looks to government to direct society, or defend a nation built on the belief that individuals should be free to pursue their own aspirations?

The growing willingness of young Americans to challenge the Left’s assumptions should be welcomed as a sign of a healthy republic. No generation is obligated to accept socialism simply because it is presented as compassionate or inevitable. Young Americans have every right to question the Left’s promises, reject its prescriptions, and choose a different path.

>>> The Cost of Growing Up: Why Gen Z Feels Priced Out of the American Dream

At The Heritage Foundation, I see why preparing the next generation to defend America’s founding principles matters. Those principles do not survive on their own. They depend on young Americans who understand what is at stake and are willing to stand up for individual liberty, free enterprise, and limited government—even when doing so puts them at odds with the prevailing political culture.

Conservatives must make that case with conviction. We must demonstrate why the American tradition offers a better vision than the Left’s growing faith in government power. We must also ensure young Americans have the confidence and knowledge to defend that vision on their campuses and in their communities.

But the Left must answer for its own conduct. If its ideas are so compelling, why respond to young Americans who reject them with threats of prosecution? If socialism offers a better future, why should its advocates fear a generation willing to challenge it?

Slotkin’s remarks expose the danger of a political movement that increasingly treats ideological opposition as something to suppress rather than an argument to win. The threat is not simply that young Americans may be discouraged from joining an administration. It is that political participation itself could become a source of fear when the wrong people hold power.

Gen Z does not owe the Left its allegiance, and no political movement has the right to intimidate young Americans into submission.

The future of the American experiment depends on a generation willing to think independently, reject failed ideologies, and defend the freedoms that make this country exceptional. If the Left cannot win that generation through its ideas, it has no business trying to scare it into silence.

#7686. Religious Liberty, Terrorist Ideology, and the Limits of School Choice

Last year, Texas enacted one of the country's most expansive school-choice policies. The Texas Education Freedom Accounts program now serves more than 100,000 students, enabling families to choose the learning environments that align with their values and best meet their children’s learning needs.

School choice at this scale is worth celebrating. School-choice policies reflect the Constitution’s commitment to religious liberty and America’s longstanding recognition that parents, not the state, are the primary educators of their children.

A century ago, the Supreme Court struck down a Ku Klux Klan-backed Oregon law that would have banned private schooling, ruling in Pierce v. Society of Sisters that “the child is not the mere creature of the state.” Parents, the Court recognized, have the right and primary authority “to direct the upbringing and education” of their children.

Half a century later, in Yoder v. Wisconsin, the Court reaffirmed the “fundamental interest of parents to guide the religious future and education of their children.” The Court declared that only “interests of the highest order” can override these fundamental freedoms.

The Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue (2020) and Carson v. Makin (2022) decisions built on that foundation, holding that states cannot exclude otherwise qualified private schools from generally available scholarship programs merely because they are religious. The Court ruled that such discrimination is “odious to the Constitution.”

But Texas policymakers are now facing a question that school-choice advocates cannot avoid: What if parents choose schools funded by foreign adversaries that indoctrinate students to hate people who are not like them, and whose founders and staff have documented ties to terrorist organizations?

>>> School Choice Is About Religious Liberty, Not Just Better Test Scores

What is the limit of school choice?

Earlier this year, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott drew a line when he declared: “There’s no school choice for schools with ties to organizations that have connections to terrorism.” Several months earlier, Abbott had designated the Muslim Brotherhood and the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) as foreign terrorist organizations. (CAIR is challenging that designation.)

After those designations, acting comptroller Kelly Hancock wrote to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton asking whether schools with ties to those organizations or the Chinese government could be excluded from the TEFA program. Paxton’s reply was unambiguous: “Let me be crystal clear: Texans’ tax dollars should never fund Islamic terrorists or America’s enemies.” Hancock then announced no schools with such ties would receive Texas tax dollars through TEFA.

That principle—that public funds should not flow to schools with ties to terrorist organizations or hostile foreign powers—is sound. All freedoms have limits. Liberty is not license. A state has a compelling interest in ensuring that taxpayer dollars do not subsidize the indoctrination of children to hate America or to support terrorism.

But even the soundest principle can be implemented in an unsound, or even unconstitutional manner.

In March 2026, Houston-area attorney and father Mehdi Cherkaoui filed a federal lawsuit against Paxton, Hancock, and Texas Education Commissioner Mike Morath, alleging that state officials had “systematically targeted Islamic schools for exclusion based on their religious identity.” His complaint observed that as of early 2026, hundreds of private schools across Texas—including numerous Christian schools—had been approved for TEFA, while not a single accredited Islamic school had been admitted. Cherkaoui sought to use TEFA funds to cover his children’s tuition at the Houston Quran Academy, but the school was not approved under the program. Three Islamic schools and additional parents joined a second suit shortly thereafter.

State officials denied the discrimination charge, explaining to the court that the comptroller’s office “had issues with processing and reviewing schools accredited by the nonprofit Cognia, regardless of whether they have Islamic affiliations.”

U.S. District Judge Alfred H. Bennett was not satisfied with that explanation. On March 17, hours before the original application deadline, he issued a temporary restraining order. At the emergency hearing, Bennett called the complete absence of approved Islamic schools “troubling,” remarking: “If you were to roll dice in a game of chance… you would not come up with those numbers. The appearance of this reeks.” He extended the student application deadline to March 31 and ordered state officials to receive and process applications from Islamic schools through the normal TEFA process. Within days, four Islamic schools were admitted: Brighter Horizons Academy in Garland, Bayaan Academy, Excellence Academy near Plano, and the Houston Quran Academy.

If it is true that the Muslim schools were not approved solely due to their religious affiliation, that would be a clear violation of their First Amendment rights. The Constitution’s guarantee of religious liberty undoubtedly prohibits such blanket discrimination.

However, the story is not so clear-cut. Two of the four schools now receiving TEFA funds—Brighter Horizons and the Houston Quran Academy—are at the center of serious, documented concerns regarding their institutional histories and affiliations.

Brighter Horizons Academy, based in Garland, is a subsidiary of the Islamic Services Foundation. According to a detailed investigation by the Middle East Forum (MEF), the school was established in part by Rasmi Almallah, who served on the board of the Holy Land Foundation—the largest terrorism financing operation in American history—and was named an unindicted co-conspirator in its 2008 federal trial.

ISF’s 2001 tax filings listed Mufid Abdelqader, a convicted HLF official and the brother of senior Hamas leader Khaled Mishal, as vice-president. His niece, Sarah Abdulqader, is currently a teacher at Brighter Horizons, and MEF notes that she “has been a passionate supporter of her convicted Hamas-financing father.” Previous staff reportedly included ISF director Nabil Sadoun, the lead author of ISF textbooks used at Brighter Horizons, a Jordanian Islamist activist whom the Dallas Morning News reported was “deported from the United States in 2010 for concealing Hamas ties on immigration paperwork.”

Some content in those ISF textbooks, used at Brighter Horizons and numerous other Islamic schools, is deeply troubling. According to MEF, one textbook teaches children ages seven and eight that non-Muslims are “the worst of creatures.” Another stresses the importance of jihad [the war against non-believers], stating: “When Muslims gave up jihad, did not abide by God’s will, started fighting among themselves and were submissive in the face of their enemies, God caused them to suffer greatly by allowing them to be dominated by those who do not fear Him or have any mercy for Islam.” The textbooks praise figures listed as unindicted co-conspirators in the Holy Land Foundation terror financing trial, including one who “describes suicide bombers and Hamas terrorists as ‘freedom fighters’ and ‘martyrs.’”

The school’s foreign funding adds another dimension. The Foundation for Defense of Democracies reported that Brighter Horizons received approximately $995,000 from the Islamic Development Bank for construction and expansion. Iran, a U.S.-designated state sponsor of terrorism, holds a significant capital share in the Islamic Development Bank and has representation on its governing board. During the Second Intifada, the bank directly managed funds that were paid to families of Palestinian terrorists who had been killed, injured, or imprisoned.

The Houston Quran Academy is operated by the Muslim American Society’s Katy Center (MAS). Federal prosecutors have described MAS as “the overt arm of the Muslim Brotherhood in the United States.” The academy’s principal, Hamed Ghazali, also chairs MAS’s Council of Islamic Schools. In 1988, Ghazali appeared to solicit funds for organizations later found to have financed Hamas. The next year, he “openly defended calls for the killing of Salman Rushdie.” In 2019, members of Congress called for an investigation into a MAS Philadelphia branch after it hosted an event in which children sang about torturing and beheading Jews.

>>> Stop Writing Blank Checks to Campuses That Protect Hate

These are not isolated cases. Middle East Forum data counts almost 800 Islamic educational initiatives across the United States, of which a clear majority are under Islamist control. Ninety of these institutions are in Texas, and several dozen may benefit from the new school subsidy program. Across those schools, MEF investigators found staff members who have shared Hamas propaganda, praised convicted terrorists, called for the destruction of America, and had children pledge loyalty to the Iranian supreme leader. Much of this infrastructure is tied to foreign money and foreign movements.

These are investigative findings, not criminal convictions against the schools themselves. But they are serious enough that state officials were right to ask questions. The comptroller’s supposed initial approach—a blanket exclusion of all Islamic schools—collides with the Constitution’s guarantee of free exercise of religion. Judge Bennett was right to find that troubling. But a blanket approval driven by litigation is also troubling.

The solution to an overbroad exclusion is not a rubber stamp, but due diligence. States must comply with the Constitution while protecting against terrorism. That requires examining each applicant school on its own record. Some Islamic schools clearly should qualify for the TEFA program. Whether Brighter Horizons and the Houston Quran Academy belong there is a harder question, and one the state should be able to answer through genuine investigation rather than blanket exclusion or court-compelled approval.

States should provide families access to robust school-choice options while protecting religious liberty. State officials should also take their duty seriously to avoid funding schools with genuine ties to terrorism. Those goals are not mutually exclusive. They require only that officials be precise, consistent, and willing to do their homework.

Before Texas state Sen. Nathan Johnson, D-Dallas, unleashed a “blue spirit bomb” on opponent Mayes Middleton on Tuesday night in the midterm elections for the Texas attorney general spot, the Thompson Coburn lawyer composed musical scores for Dragon Ball Z, a Japanese anime series about martial artists who defend the world from destruction.

A piano player, Johnson learned how to write music while working as a lawyer and liked it so much that he decided to quit his job and focus on doing film and television composition, according to the article.

Johnson eventually went back to law and started a solo practice. While looking for office space, he met a landlord connected to a Texas company that licensed the English version of Dragon Ball Z in the United States. The company then hired Johnson in the early 2000s, according to Chron.com.

“It gave me a creative outlet and a cultural connection that very few people have had the opportunity to have,” Johnson said in an interview, according to Variety.

#7683. School Districts' Negligence and Nuisance Claims Against Social Media Companies Rejected by California Court of Appeal

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Some short excerpts from the long decision Thursday in Social Media Cases (San Diego Unified School Dist. v. Meta Platforms, Inc.) by California Court of Appeal Justice Anne Richardson, joined by Justices Elwood Lui and Stephen Goorvitch):

In recent years, various plaintiffs have brought numerous legal claims against social media companies. In this opinion, we address only two causes of action—negligence and public nuisance—in the context of the laws of California, Florida, Washington, and Rhode Island, brought by school districts…. Plaintiffs generally claimed Defendants created a "mental health crisis" among their students that harmed Plaintiffs by disrupting their educational mission, requiring them to spend more money and staff time to address student mental health and discipline, and causing students to vandalize their property….

We acknowledge the serious allegations of mental health harms experienced by many students and the impact of those harms on Plaintiffs' schools and student bodies…. [But the relevant precedents] establish that these plaintiffs cannot proceed under the legal theories and factual allegations they have pled….

Here, Plaintiffs allege they suffered three general kinds of harm: (1) "incur[ring] significant financial costs" to address the youth mental health crisis allegedly created by Defendants' platforms; (2) "frustrat[ion] [of their] pedagogical mission" in diverting staff time and resources from education to counter the disruptive effects of the crisis; and (3) property damage inflicted by students. In part V., we conclude Plaintiffs' allegations their missions were frustrated do not state a cognizable negligence claim, and in part VI., we conclude Defendants have immunity from liability arising from Plaintiffs' alleged property damage. {Plaintiffs do not allege Defendants directly damaged their property; instead, they allege Defendants' platforms influenced students to vandalize school property because the platforms showed them so-called "challenge videos," created by third parties, that encouraged vandalizing school property. The trial court determined [47 U.S.C. § 230] provided Defendants immunity from liability arising from the challenge videos. We agree.}

That leaves Plaintiffs with only alleged financial harms …. The crux of the negligence causes of action is the applicability of the so-called "economic loss rule." … "… In general, there is no recovery in tort for negligently inflicted 'purely economic losses,' meaning financial harm unaccompanied by physical or property damage" [even as to foreseeable economic losses -EV]…. "[A]ssume[ ] a defendant negligently causes an automobile accident that blocks a major traffic artery such as a bridge or tunnel. Although defendant would be liable for personal injuries and property damage suffered in such an accident, it is doubtful any court would allow recovery by the myriad of third parties who might claim economic losses because the bridge or tunnel was impassible." …

Nuisance suits are generally either public or private. "[A] private nuisance is a civil wrong based on disturbance of rights in land[,] while a public nuisance is [based] upon an interference with the rights of the community at large."

"Nuisance has been described as an 'impenetrable jungle'" that "'mean[s] all things to all people'" and "'is incapable of any exact or comprehensive definition.'" Thus, while nuisance is often defined broadly, many courts have limited its scope in practice. For example, the Washington Supreme Court expressly limits nuisance claims "to property infringement [and] threats to health and safety." Some of our fellow Courts of Appeal have prohibited bringing products liability claims in the guise of public nuisance actions.

Such limits are often imposed because of a concern that "nuisance 'would [otherwise] become a monster that would devour in one gulp the entire law of tort.'" In the products liability context, "'[a]ll a creative mind would need to do is construct a scenario describing a known or perceived harm … that can somehow be said to relate back to the way a company … makes, markets and/or sells its non-defective, lawful product or service, and a public nuisance claim would be conceived and born.'"

The trial court concluded Plaintiffs failed to adequately plead public nuisance because the harms alleged to have befallen individual student users of Defendants' platforms did not amount to a public nuisance, even when "considered collectively." While our analysis may differ from the trial court's in some particulars, we ultimately agree Plaintiffs' efforts to state a cause of action for public nuisance fail under the laws of California, Washington, and Florida….

California nuisance is broadly defined by statute as "[a]nything which is injurious to health, including, but not limited to, the illegal sale of controlled substances, or is indecent or offensive to the senses, or an obstruction to the free use of property, so as to interfere with the comfortable enjoyment of life or property, or unlawfully obstructs the free passage or use, in the customary manner, of any navigable lake, or river, bay, stream, canal, or basin, or any public park, square, street, or highway, is a nuisance."

Public nuisance is defined by statute as "one which affects at the same time an entire community or neighborhood, or any considerable number of persons, although the extent of the annoyance or damage inflicted upon individuals may be unequal." "[P]ublic nuisances are offenses against, or interferences with, the exercise of rights common to the public." "It is [the] community aspect of the public nuisance … that distinguishes it from its private cousin," and makes it suitable "to protect the quality of organized social life."

Perhaps because of those broad definitions, our Legislature has codified who has standing to bring a public nuisance action. Certain persons may bring an action for public nuisance when it is "specially injurious" to them or when their property is "injuriously affected or [their] personal enjoyment is lessened."

By contrast, a "public body or officer authorized thereto" can bring an action to abate a public nuisance. And the State or designated county or city officials, in their representative capacities, can bring an action limited to abatement under Code of Civil Procedure section 731. San Diego's action, however, is not limited to abatement, but seeks damages for harms allegedly caused by the nuisance. The only recognized exception to the limitation on remedy is that a public entity may seek damages when it sues in its role as a property owner.

While San Diego makes a number of arguments related to its public nuisance theory, some of which have divided our fellow Courts of Appeal, we need not parse them in detail because San Diego failed to adequately allege its standing to bring a public nuisance cause of action….

San Diego first argues it has standing under Civil Code section 3493. That statute expressly allows "[a] private person" to bring a public nuisance action…. [G]overnment entities are not "private person[s]" for purposes of section 3493….

In the alternative, San Diego argues it may bring a public nuisance cause of action pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 731. That statute provides "[a]n action may be brought by any person whose property is injuriously affected, or whose personal enjoyment is lessened by a nuisance, as defined in Section 3479 of the Civil Code," and damages may be recovered. …

San Diego's complaint did not adequately plead its property was "injuriously affected" or its "personal enjoyment [was] lessened" by the alleged nuisance of Defendants' platforms…. Rather, the complaint's focus throughout its 286 pages is on the "unprecedented mental health crisis" among students and its disruption to schools' public educational mission…. Any connection to property here is abstract at best.

Accepting San Diego's position would convert virtually any personal injury affecting a property owner into a nuisance. For example, consider a homeowner whose son breaks his leg in a car accident with a negligent driver, rendering him unable to use the stairs in the home. Even if the homeowner must spend time and resources to help her son navigate the home, she has no nuisance cause of action against the driver on the ground the driver interfered with her use and enjoyment of her property….

Because all Plaintiffs' causes of action fail for the reasons discussed, we do not consider whether they are entirely barred by section 230 and the First Amendment to the United States Constitution….

Jonathan H. Blavin and Victoria A. Degtyareva (Munger, Tolles & Olson), Paul J. Watford, Bailey J. Langner, David P. Mattern and Geoffrey M. Drake (King & Spalding), Mark W. Mosier, Ashley M. Simonsen and Christian J. Pistilli (Covington & Burling), and Ashley W. Hardin, George A. Borden and Neelum J. Wadhwani (Williams & Connolly) represent defendants.

NEXT: Disability Discrimination and Allegations of AI Use in Student's University of Michigan Course Papers

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7682. Philadelphia Is Dusting Off the Subprime Playbook

Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle Parker wants to make her city the first in the nation to offer a city-backed mortgage, available to people who wouldn’t otherwise qualify for a loan. If that sounds familiar, it’s because loosening lending standards was the recipe for the housing bubble of the early 2000s, and the City of Brotherly looks ready to bake that cake again.

Under the mayor’s One Philly Mortgage plan, first-time buyers with “less-than-perfect credit” could put down as little as 3 percent, pay no private mortgage insurance, and get an interest rate roughly 1 percentage point below market, while public funds cover part of the interest payments. If the loan goes bad, the city covers it, meaning taxpayers foot the bill.

And that bill could be quite large, judging by the mayor offering a credit score of 620 as an example of who the program will serve. That’s right on the line traditionally used to separate subprime borrowers. Lenders have good reason for preferring higher credit scores and eschewing subprime borrowers: lower scores are highly correlated with increased default risk.

Credit scores aren’t some kind of moral judgment but a statistical proxy for the likelihood that someone will repay a loan. They’re formed from decades of data across millions of loans, not opinions or feelings. Someone with a higher credit score is less likely to default on the same loan as someone with a lower score. 

Likewise, lenders use additional tools like verified income to establish whether a borrower can actually afford the proposed monthly payment, while a down payment shows the borrower has the discipline to save and gives him skin in the game. Additionally, it provides an equity cushion that protects both borrower and lender if home prices dip, which has happened in many markets over the last few years.

>>> U.S. Government-Backed Homebuying Market Drives Up House Prices for Ordinary Americans

But with the mayor’s proposed plan of only 3 percent down, that cushion is paper thin. Selling a home often costs 6 percent or more in commissions and closing costs, so a buyer with 3 percent equity is effectively underwater the day he moves in. If he loses his job or faces a big repair bill, he can’t sell his way out. That’s when defaults turn into foreclosures.

The nation already learned that lesson the hard way, but apparently Parker forgets that, in the early 2000s, Washington pushed hard to expand homeownership, and lenders relaxed their standards to oblige. Down payments shrank, credit requirements loosened, and “liar loans” that skipped income verification became commonplace.

By 2006, roughly one in five new mortgages was subprime. When interest rates rose and home prices stopped rising, the defaults came in waves, millions of families lost their homes, and taxpayers were left footing the bill for bailouts by the Treasury and Federal Reserve, most of which just benefited Wall Street.

Banks ordinarily underwrite loans carefully because they bear the risk of default. Even if they sell a loan, they get top dollar for it when the default risk is low, so there’s still an incentive to lend carefully. When government promises to cover losses, however, that prudence disappears.

Under Parker’s scheme, the banks get to collect interest, some of which is paid for by taxpayers, and then those lenders don’t have to worry about losses because taxpayers will cover those too if they arrive. It’s privatized profits and socialized losses—no wonder Citizens Bank wants to participate! That’s what made the last bubble so destructive, and it’s exactly what a loan loss reserve does.

The mayor may have the best of intentions, but there’s an infamous road constructed with those. And while supporters point to a Massachusetts program that is supposedly both similar and successful, that hasn’t been without costs to taxpayers either. Nor is it necessarily comparable to what Parker’s pursuing.

>>> How to Make Housing Affordable: Build More Homes

Massachusetts households earn far more than Philadelphia’s, and Philadelphia’s housing stock is older and more distressed. What works in Boston’s suburbs won’t necessarily work in Kensington—they’re fundamentally different markets.

Philadelphia has one of the highest poverty rates of any big city in America. Even Drexel economist Kevin Gillen warns that expanding homeownership through risky lending without addressing poverty and distressed housing could raise foreclosure rates, especially when buyers take on repairs they can’t afford.

It’s true that housing affordability has deteriorated badly in recent years, including in Philadelphia, where it now takes 47 percent of the median household’s pre-tax income to cover the monthly mortgage payment on a median-priced home. But that answer isn’t putting taxpayers on the hook for loans that private lenders would never make on their own.

Instead of creating a subprime bubble, the city could reduce property taxes and permitting delays or enact zoning reform to make building and living in Philadelphia more affordable. Unfortunately, cutting taxes or red tape doesn’t lend itself to a flashy interview for the mayor the way subsidizing irresponsible lending does. Besides, taxpayers won’t see the final bill for years.

#7681. Freedom Isn’t Automatic—Each Generation Must Fight To Keep It

President Ronald Reagan’s famous warning that “Freedom is never more than one generation away from extinction; it has to be fought for and defended by each generation” is even more relevant today than when he first said it.

He correctly identified that prosperity is not a predetermined outcome. It is created and sustained by culture, institutions, and economic freedom, and it must therefore be the responsibility of every generation to protect and preserve it.

The comforting but misguided belief in economic determinism—holding that prosperity is determined by geography, natural resources, or historical circumstances—must be rejected. By this logic, the United States was destined to be a superpower simply because it occupies a resource-rich continent and is protected by two oceans.

Natural resources and geography may create opportunities, but they do not guarantee prosperity. History shows that Americans have intentionally pursued free enterprise, transparent institutions, and a limited federal government system that transformed opportunity into prosperity and allowed the nation to flourish.

The myth of economic determinism can be revealed by one of history’s most compelling natural experiments: North Korea and South Korea. The stark development trajectories between the two is evidence that political choices impact national outcomes. After World War II, North and South shared a common culture, language, geography, and history, yet chose dramatically different political and economic systems.

>>> The Surprising New Guardians Of Liberty And What It Means For The Left

South Korea embraced free enterprise, international trade, and economic liberation. North Korea adopted central planning, state ownership, and authoritarian rule. One developed into one of the world’s most advanced economies with residents enjoying personal freedoms and prosperity, while the other remains impoverished and isolated.

This contrast is even visible from space. Satellite photographs show South Korea illuminated at night by extensive infrastructure and a vibrant city, while North Korea remains dark due to an undeveloped power grid, poor infrastructure, and political factors that prioritize military needs over civilian energy consumption.

Geography didn’t create that divergence—communist policies did.

Similarly, Venezuela was among the wealthiest nations in Latin America for much of the 20th century, driven by large oil reserves. If natural resources guaranteed prosperity, it would be among the richest countries today. Instead, Venezuela fell from one of the most prosperous South American countries to one of the least prosperous in the world, with the Fraser Institute’s Economic Freedom Index ranking Venezuela number 22nd globally in 1980 and number 165th in 2021.

In less than half a century, empty promises made by socialist policymakers and enacted big-government policies undermined Venezuela’s economic foundation. The Manhattan Institute finds three policies implemented by dictator Hugo Chavez responsible for the nation’s widespread economic and humanitarian crisis: “nationalization of private industry, currency and price controls, and the fiscally irresponsible expansion of welfare programs.”

Chavez first nationalized agriculture by taking wealth and property from landowners and giving it to workers—leading to mismanagement and destruction of those resources. He then implemented controls to keep prices artificially low, which pushed out remaining firms and led to nationalized central authority. Finally, he expanded welfare programs purported to address poverty, educational shortcomings, and healthcare; all financed through high taxation and currency printing to the point of hyperinflation.

Inflation spiked, shortages of food and medicine became commonplace, government dependence increased, investment collapsed, and millions emigrated out of the country in search of better opportunities.

>>> The Conservative Coalition We Need to Save the West

But remember, in 1998 Chavez was democratically elected president. He campaigned on providing relief to poor- and middle-class populations by redistributing oil wealth in the form of social services—awfully similar to the “tax the rich” slogans of American socialists today. What starts with government programs, free buses, and artificially lower grocery prices ends with centralized authority, overreach, and the very socialist regimes that have killed citizens and destroyed entire countries in practice.

The lesson is that prosperity depends on policy—and this fact is increasingly relevant in the United States.

Socialist ideology has already made its way to America’s blue cities, with the youth driving this ideological shift from capitalism to socialism. Their affordability grievances are real, yet history repeatedly demonstrates that concentrated power in the hands of the state risks liberty, innovation, and long-term prosperity.

America’s future is not guaranteed. It depends on whether future generations defend and renew the principles and economic systems that historically made America great. Individual freedoms, economic mobility, and national prosperity should not be considered expectations, but rather privileges of ordered policies and culture.

That’s why policymakers and citizens must constantly, intentionally agitate for limited and constitutional government, a strong rule of law, and free enterprise to secure America’s future—because as Reagan reminded us, economic destiny is not guaranteed. It’s fought for and won time and time again.

#7680. How To Win Back the Disillusioned American Dream

Conservatives often assume socialism is easy to defeat. After all, the failing historical record of central planning and the economic success of free markets are on their side. But that hasn’t stopped socialism from gaining ground, particularly among young Americans.

A Fox News poll finds that while 72% of Democrats under the age of 45 believe capitalism is not working well, 66% think moving to socialism would be a good idea. Those numbers should concern any American who values economic freedom.

Many older conservatives immediately respond by pointing to the Soviet Union, Venezuela, or Cuba as evidence of the horrors of socialism. They’re not wrong, but they’re not addressing the question young voters are actually asking.

Young people are choosing socialism not because they hate America, but because they believe the once reliable American Dream is out of reach. Homeownership is becoming unattainable. Student debt delays major life decisions. Family formation is becoming more expensive every year. Upward mobility seems impossible when wages barely outpace inflation.

Their frustration is real, and though the promises of socialism are empty, those of capitalism—or at least what they think is capitalism—have gone unfulfilled.

The median sales price of a new home was over $410,000 in 2025, nearly five times the median household income, a ratio almost twice as high as in 1980. Student loans cost the average new graduate hundreds of dollars per month. And despite inflation coming down from pandemic peaks, 3.4% CPI eats away at weekly paychecks.

>>> The Cost of Growing Up: Why Gen Z Feels Priced Out of the American Dream

Simply put, the cost of adulthood has become unaffordable for millions of young Americans.

Socialists have recognized this reality, and though their proposed solutions are economically unsustainable, at least they acknowledge the problem. And too often, conservatives are quick to condemn socialism without addressing the underlying reasons why Gen Z finds it attractive.

Socialists blame capitalism for modern economic hardship, but the affordability crisis should not be treated as evidence that competitive capitalism is failing America’s youth. In most sectors burdening young Americans, competition has been weakened by government intervention, political favoritism, and policies that distort prices and restrict supply.

Look at housing. For decades, local governments restricted development with zoning regulations, permitting delays, and other barriers to construction. Simultaneously, government-backed mortgage policies increased purchasing power without addressing supply shortages. Then, politicians responded to rising costs with rent control and rent freezes that further distorted the market and drove up homeownership costs.

It’s no surprise, then, that the average age of a first-time homebuyer is at an all-time high of 40.

Next, look to higher education. Government-backed student lending has enabled colleges to raise prices. The result is a system that saddles students with tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars of debt and politicians that propose student loan forgiveness or other subsidies as the solution—which neither adds value to the credential, lowers the cost of providing education, nor changes the broken mechanism behind why college tuition is so expensive.

The housing and college markets are not examples of a free market operating properly. They reflect government-created scarcity, regulatory dysfunction, and cronyism.

Therefore, cost-of-living concerns facing Gen Z should not be used as evidence that competitive capitalism is a failed model—especially when most economic problems stem from policies fundamentally opposed to the free market.

For policymakers, this means acknowledging Gen Z’s reasonable concerns and showing them how freedom, not government control, can improve life.

>>> The Surprising New Guardians Of Liberty And What It Means For The Left

When conservatives respond to rising socialist affiliation only by warning about unsuccessful experiments, they fail to address the affordability problems people experience every day, which are driving this ideological shift.

The average American is not watching lectures on the historical failures of central planning or reading through textbooks comparing the economic philosophies of Karl Marx and Adam Smith. Young Americans are instead trying to make monthly rent payments, budget to buy a house, pay back student loans, and afford groceries—all while entering adulthood, starting a career, and raising a family.

So, a successful conservative strategy must both demonstrate how free-market policies solve modern problems and expose the socioeconomic failures of socialism.

This means increasing housing supply, removing government distortions in housing and other markets, lowering barriers to entrepreneurship, promoting energy abundance, reducing regulatory burdens, and making family formation more affordable. Most importantly, Americans need evidence that economic freedom reliably produces upward mobility.

The greatest victories against socialism were never won through slogans, but through prosperity. When people can afford homes, start businesses, raise families, and build wealth, socialism loses its appeal. But when those opportunities disappear, socialism gains favor.

The future debate over socialism won’t be won by arguing endlessly about 20th-century failed experiments in foreign nations. It will be won by proving that economic freedom can still deliver opportunity and prosperity for all Americans in the 21st century.

#7678. New York’s Property Tax Hike Chases Wealthy Wallets Away

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani faces an uphill battle balancing the city’s budget while ushering in his very expensive socialist utopia. But rest assured: New public bathrooms and free opera tickets are still coming, and the ultra-wealthy will foot the bill. Or so the plan goes. Predictably, his “tax the rich” mantra is already going beyond New York socialites.

With the pied-à-terre tax implemented in July, property owners and investors who simply maintain a secondary residence in one of the city’s boroughs are subject to a new property tax surcharge. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul proposed it on April 15 to help close the city’s budget gap—the same day Mr. Mamdani posted a video outside Citadel CEO Ken Griffin’s $238 million penthouse, naming him as an example.

The legislature approved the measure on May 27, and it took effect on July 1. It expires June 30, 2031, unless renewed. In the first phase, which runs through mid-2028, condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more face new, steep tax rates of 4% to 6.5%. For context, New York state’s average effective property tax rate in 2024 was 1.3% and Manhattan’s was 0.71%.

Mr. Mamdani’s “fair share” philosophy includes a quintupling of property taxes on thousands of people. After that initial phase, the surcharge threshold rises to $5 million with lower rates of 0.8% to 1.3% applying to all non-primary residences, exempting housing units under arm’s length leases of at least one year.

>>> No, Mamdani, Socialism Does Not Increase Affordability

Even these lower rates will double people’s property taxes. Furthermore, the lower rates are designed to be offset by new valuation methods being cooked up by the city Department of Finance to increase the assessed value of properties.

The rollout was messy from the start, when the city published a list of 900,000 high-value properties along with many of the owners’ full names. The city appeared to adopt a kind of guilty-until-proven-innocent tax liability, making residents argue they aren’t subject to the pied- à-terre tax. Owners were left with confusion and a loss of privacy.

Since Manhattan has roughly 16,700 condos and co-ops valued above the $1 million threshold, it will be hit hardest by this tax. Secondary residents will owe an average surcharge of $68,559 each year. Brooklyn also shows significant exposure, with the outer boroughs coming in at smaller counts.

New York projects the measure will raise about $500 million in annual revenue. But that assumes the owners stay. Revenue could easily fall by tens of millions of dollars if some owners leave and sell off their secondary residences, which is why wealth taxes elsewhere have repeatedly fallen short of projections. Each property owner who leaves the city shrinks the tax base.

Ultimately, this is a tax on investment in New York real estate with ramifications that will affect even middle-class New Yorkers. Picture a wealthy Californian considering a second residence on the East Coast. #7676. New Mexico Supreme Court permanently disbars prosecutor after disciplinary findings

The New Mexico Supreme Court, after hearing from a disciplinary board, has permanently disbarred a prosecutor who was found to have pattern of misconduct that denied defendants fair trials. (Image from Shutterstock)

The New Mexico Supreme Court, after hearing from a disciplinary board, has permanently disbarred a prosecutor who was found to have pattern of misconduct that denied defendants fair trials.

Cosme Ripol, a prosecutor from the district attorney’s office for the Eighth Judicial District in Taos, New Mexico, was disbarred Monday, effective immediately.

All five justices on the state supreme court agreed on the disciplinary board’s recommendation. The proceedings focused on three criminal cases that Ripol prosecuted between 2022 and 2024.

According to coverage by the Santa Fe New Mexican, a pivotal case in the investigation was State v. Desiree Lensegrav, where the defendant was convicted in 2022 of first-degree murder, kidnapping, conspiracy and tampering with evidence.

The New Mexico Supreme Court vacated Lensegrav’s convictions after it learned that Ripol, who had been licensed to practice law in the state since 1986, used inadmissible evidence and made derogatory statements about the defendant during the trial.

“As the supreme court noted, prosecutors are held to a higher standard because of their unique responsibility to seek justice,” said Marcus Montoya, the district attorney for the Eighth Judicial District, in a statement Monday. “When improper tactics are employed in the courtroom, even by an attorney with more than 30 years of criminal law experience, that standard is not met.”

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

"Going forward, the path of advancing the conservative legal movement requires a political reorientation."

My new essay in Civitas tries to make sense of how the midterm election affects the broader conservative legal movement. Here is the introduction:

President Donald Trump's surprise 2016 election saved Justice Antonin Scalia's seat and perhaps the Supreme Court. Over the ensuing decade, Trump appointed scores of originalist judges at all levels of the judiciary and led a political movement that supported originalist state court judges and attorneys general. But that movement came to a screeching halt with the 2026 midterm election. Indeed, the blue tsunami, largely a referendum on Trump, threatens to drown originalism. In deep red states, conservative judges were washed off the bench. Also swept from office were conservative governors who appoint judges and attorneys general who litigate in those courts. Given the large Democratic Senate majority and unfavorable maps for 2028 and 2030, a Republican Senate with the votes to confirm originalist judges may not return until 2033 at the earliest. An entire generation of talent will be wasted. A necessary condition for a successful legal movement is a successful political party. Legal conservatives need to carefully reconsider the political circumstances best suited to defend the Constitution.

The conservative legal movement has always existed in conjunction and disjunction with the broader conservative political movement.  Certain long-term projects concerning the separation of powers and individual rights endure regardless of who is in office, but legal disputes arise with the exigencies of the day. The conservative legal movement will often, but not always, coalesce around current conservative political needs. Likewise, the conservative political movement will often, but not always, coalesce around the conservative legal movement. During two recent events, Justice Elena Kagan recognized this dichotomy. She observed that conservative members of the Supreme Court decide cases that are right "out of the playbook of the conservative legal movement," even as some of President Trump's policies suffer setbacks in the courts. Indeed, Trump has repeatedly expressed frustration that his appointees rule against him.

Many legal conservatives came to terms with voting for Trump in 2016 as a way to save the Supreme Court. Many more legal conservatives came around to Trump in 2020 based on his track record of appointing originalist judges--although I think that record is overstated. When Trump was on the ballot in 2024, some legal conservatives supported Trump for fear that Kamala Harris would pack the Supreme Court. But 2026 altered the calculus. Trump, and those candidates he endorsed, were routed in red states. Moreover, conservative judges and attorney generals were wiped from office. When the top of the ticket is no longer able to win elections, downballot judges and attorneys general do not stand a chance. Red states can only bleed for so long until they turn blue. A necessary condition for a successful legal movement is a political party that can produce viable candidates. Going forward, the path of advancing the conservative legal movement requires a political reorientation. The conservative legal movement can only survive if conservative lawyers are in public office to move the law. The blue tsunami cannot be allowed to drown originalism.

NEXT: School Districts' Negligence and Nuisance Claims Against Social Media Companies Rejected by California Court of Appeal

Josh Blackman is a constitutional law professor at the South Texas College of Law Houston and the President of the Harlan Institute. Follow him @JoshMBlackman.

#7674. California’s Potential Billionaire Tax Has Already Cost The State

California’s latest proposed tax increase has already led to so much wealth fleeing the state that tax revenue is set to fall, not rise. Golden State politicians announced the upcoming opening day of hunting season on billionaires and are about to find out they can’t fund welfare programs by taxing people who have already left.

At issue is California’s Proposition 40, a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ net worth, which proponents claim will raise $100 billion for state-funded health care. Unfortunately for them, the wealthy were paying attention. At least seven high-profile billionaires left the state before Jan. 1 of this year, the residency date that determines who owes the tax.

They took with them roughly $539 billion of the state’s $1.9 trillion in billionaire wealth. Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin alone shrank the expected haul by $25 billion.

The fact is, $100 billion was never a realistic revenue projection. That estimate ignored losses from departures and legal challenges and both are certain to keep coming. The retroactive residency date alone invites a raft of constitutional challenges.

Supreme Court precedent bars retroactively imposing a “wholly new tax.” Locking people into paying whether they stay or leave, before voters have even approved the tax, burdens the constitutional right to travel. And as the Tax Foundation notes, uncapped penalties on appraisers of hard-to-value assets raise Excessive Fines Clause concerns, since they’re grossly disproportionate to good-faith errors.

>>> California Risks Killing the Golden Goose With Proposition 40

Once departures and litigation are counted, Stanford economists Joshua Rauh and Benjamin Jaros estimate the tax would bring in closer to $30 billion. That’s less than one-third of what was promised, which is bad news for Medi-Cal, the state’s Medicaid program.

But the bigger problem has already arrived. While a wealth tax is collected once, an income tax is collected every year. Rauh and Jaros estimate California’s billionaires pay between $3.3 billion and $5.8 billion in state income tax annually, and every billionaire who relocates takes his share with him permanently.

Weigh that lost income tax revenue against Prop 40’s one-time haul, and the net present value of the tax comes out to negative $38.9 billion.

In other words, the tax is a money-loser for the state. And this estimate isn’t a mere outlier from unlikely assumptions: economists ran 100,000 simulations with different revenue estimates and discount rates, and the state came out behind in 85% of them.

California already depends on a sliver of total earners for most of its tax receipts, with the top 1 percent of earners supplying roughly half of all personal income tax revenue. These are the people creating business, funding startups, and employing thousands of Californians. Losing even a handful of them does real damage to state and family finances alike.

>>> New York’s Property Tax Hike Chases Wealthy Wallets Away

Ironically, the billionaires who flee suffer less than the average Californian. As F. Scott Fitzgerald said, the rich are different from you and me; they can leave for Florida, Tennessee, Texas, or another low-tax state. It’s California’s public services, funded by their income, that will suffer.

Medi-Cal and the other programs counting on this money will still need funding. When $100 billion becomes $30 billion, followed by a permanent reduction to income tax revenue, politicians will clamor for more tax hikes.

But with a shrinking tax base of billionaires, the hikes will inevitably fall on the middle class. A tax sold as making billionaires “pay their fair share” will end up costing the residents not wealthy enough to leave.

Supporters will point to research showing high-earners rarely move because of taxes. But the best-known study examined ordinary income tax rates over many years. A levy on someone’s entire net worth is a different animal and will prompt more people to leave, as seven just did.

Before Californians vote on Prop 40, they should understand how much the tax will realistically raise—and who will get stuck with the actual bill in the long run.
